name: Cognitrel
description: Cognitrel is a broad-spectrum cognitive support compound that works by partitioning working memory resources more efficiently, allowing the brain to maintain multiple active task-states simultaneously without the typical performance degradation that accompanies task-switching. It is the workhorse drug of the Tier 2 and Tier 3 workforce — unglamorous, reliable, and deeply embedded in the culture of people who do too many things at once.
effects: Significantly reduced cognitive cost of task-switching
Ability to maintain 3-5 parallel mental threads without interference
side_effects: Depersonalization during heavy multi-task loads — the sense of 'who is in charge' becomes diffuse
Difficulty fully disengaging from tasks post-dose
Chronic use associated with reduced ability to achieve deep single-focus states
Sleep disruption from residual task-state activation
cultural_context: Cognitrel is the most boring drug in GLMZ, and also one of the most widely used. Novafold sells it in bulk to employers who distribute it as a workplace wellness benefit — the Tier 2 equivalent of a corporate health plan. Factory supervisors, dispatch coordinators, customer-facing service workers, junior analysts — anyone whose job requires managing multiple streams simultaneously takes Cog. There is no glamour attached to it. It is a tool, like a good pair of boots. The depersonalization side effect has generated a quiet cultural phenomenon: long-term Cog users sometimes describe themselves in the plural, or refer to 'the part of me that was handling logistics' as though it were a separate entity.
story_hooks: A Tier 2 logistics coordinator has been on Cognitrel for eight years and has developed a genuine dissociative disorder — they experience themselves as a committee of task-selves, each managing a different operational thread, and they're no longer sure which one is the original.

Novafold has quietly reformulated Cognitrel to make the task-disengagement difficulty more pronounced, engineering a form of dependency that isn't classified as addiction but makes users functionally unable to manage their workload without it — the evidence is in the reformulation records, if someone can get to them.

A Cog-using dispatcher noticed something wrong in a routing pattern during a multi-task session — a discrepancy too subtle to catch at normal cognition — and now they're trying to figure out how to report it without revealing they were medicated on duty.
